mainTopic: Why idols seem to have power though they have none, and when grape juice handled by a נכרי becomes יין נסך
overview: This amud finishes a ברייתא about why God does not destroy the objects people worship as עבודה זרה. Reading a פסוק in צפניה, it explains that if God destroyed everything that is worshipped, He would have to destroy people too. Next, אגריפס the general asks רבן גמליאל how God can be 'jealous' of idols that are nothing. רבן גמליאל answers with a parable: a wife is most jealous when she is replaced by a lesser rival. Then זונין asks רבי עקיבא why sick people seem to come back healed from idol temples. רבי עקיבא answers that sufferings are sworn to leave at a set time, and they keep their oath even when the person acts foolishly. רבי יוחנן's reading of 'evil and faithful sicknesses' supports this. When an idol seems to bring rain after a human sacrifice, רב יהודה explains, using רב's teaching and ריש לקיש's teaching, that God lets those who choose sin be misled. Finally, a new משנה teaches that grape juice becomes יין נסך only once it reaches the vat, and it begins a rule about treading grapes with a נכרי that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Quoting the verse about consuming the stumbling blocks
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא quotes a פסוק in צפניה that lists the 'stumbling blocks of the wicked' (idols) among the things God could destroy.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Shall I utterly consume all things from off the face of the earth, says the Lord? Shall I consume man and beast? Shall I consume the birds of the heavens and the fish of the sea, and the stumbling blocks of the wicked, etc."
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a פסוק as support for its answer about why God does not destroy idols. This step only quotes the פסוק; the next step explains what it proves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'stumbling blocks of the wicked' are the objects of עבודה זרה that lead people to sin. The ברייתא reads the פסוק as a question God asks: 'Should I really destroy all these?' This sets up the reasoning in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Stumbling blocks: here, idols that cause people to sin
And so on: the פסוק continues

phrases.english: "Shall I utterly consume all things
phrases.notes: צפניה 1:2–3. The ברייתא reads these lines as questions God is asking.

phrases.english: from off the face of the earth, says the Lord?
Shall I consume man and beast?
Shall I consume the birds of the heavens and the fish of the sea,
and the stumbling blocks of the wicked, etc."
phrases.notes: 'Stumbling blocks' means the idols, the things that trip the wicked into sin.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָסֹף אָסֵף כֹּל מֵעַל פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה נְאֻם ה׳
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from the previous daf about why God does not destroy objects of עבודה זרה.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that God does not destroy things merely because people sin with them

steps.title: If God destroyed every worshipped thing, He would have to destroy people too
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains the פסוק: God will not destroy idols just because the wicked stumble over them, because people are also worshipped, and He will not destroy humanity.
steps.simpleTranslation: But should God wipe them out of the world just because the wicked stumble over them? Don't idol worshippers also worship people? As the פסוק continues: "And shall I cut off man from off the face of the earth?"
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא draws the lesson from the פסוק: destroying everything that is worshipped would mean destroying people too, so God leaves the world as it is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The logic is that being worshipped is not a reason for God to destroy something. Some people are treated as gods, and the end of the same פסוק shows that God would not 'cut off man.' So the existence of idols does not mean God approves of them.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it so that...: a rhetorical challenge

steps.whatToRemember: God does not destroy idols just because people worship them. If He did, He would also have to destroy people, since people are worshipped too.

phrases.english: But just because the wicked stumble over them
should He wipe them out of the world?
Don't they also worship people?
"And shall I cut off man
phrases.notes: This is the end of the same פסוק, צפניה 1:3.

phrases.english: from off the face of the earth, etc."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָרְשָׁעִים נִכְשָׁלִים בָּהֶן יְאַבְּדֵם מִן הָעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the lesson of the פסוק quoted in step 1.
steps.raayaObject: God does not destroy objects just because the wicked sin through them
steps.raayaSupportSource: The end of the פסוק: 'and I will cut off man from off the face of the earth'

steps.title: אגריפס asks why God would be jealous of powerless idols
steps.stepSummary: אגריפס the general challenges רבן גמליאל: jealousy only happens between equals, so why does the תורה call God 'jealous' of idols?
steps.simpleTranslation: אגריפס the general asked רבן גמליאל: It is written in your תורה, "For the Lord your God is a devouring fire, a jealous God." But isn't jealousy only between equals: a wise man is jealous of a wise man, a strong man of a strong man, a rich man of a rich man?
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. אגריפס points out what looks like a contradiction: if idols are nothing, how can God be jealous of them?
steps.deeperAnalysis: People only feel jealous of someone on their own level. Idols are far beneath God, so jealousy seems to make no sense, and the פסוק might even suggest that idols are real rivals. The question is shaped like a question, but it works as a challenge to the תורה's wording.

phrases.english: Agrippas the general asked
Rabban Gamliel:
It is written in your Torah:
"For the Lord your God is a devouring fire,
a jealous God."
Isn't jealousy only between a wise man and another wise man,
a strong man and another strong man, a rich man and another rich man?
phrases.notes: His point: jealousy happens between equals, and idols are not equal to God.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאַל אַגְרִיפַּס שַׂר צָבָא אֶת רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story about how God relates to idols.
steps.kashyaTarget: The פסוק calling God 'a jealous God' about idols
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Jealousy only exists between equals, and idols are not equal to God, so the jealousy seems out of place.

steps.title: רבן גמליאל's parable of the two wives
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל answers with a parable: a wife is not jealous of a more important second wife, but she is jealous of a lesser one.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I will give you a parable. What is this like? A man who married a second wife in addition to his first. If the new wife is more important than the first, the first wife is not jealous of her. If the new wife is less important, the first wife is jealous of her.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל turns אגריפס's logic upside down: jealousy is strongest when someone is replaced by something worse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אגריפס assumed jealousy happens only between equals. רבן גמליאל shows that being left for something lower hurts the most. So God's 'jealousy' is the insult of being exchanged for worthless idols. It does not mean the idols have any real importance.

keyTerms.meaning: I will give you a parable

steps.whatToRemember: God's 'jealousy' does not make idols important. It shows how insulting it is to swap God for something worthless.
steps.confusionAlert: The parable does not mean idols are God's 'rivals.' The point is the opposite: the jealousy comes from how low the idols are.

phrases.english: He said to him: I will give you a parable.
To what is the matter comparable?
To a man who married a woman in addition to his wife.
If she is more important than her, she is not jealous of her;
phrases.notes: The 'she' who is or isn't jealous is the first wife.

phrases.english: if she is less important than her, she is jealous of her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: אֶמְשׁוֹל לְךָ מָשָׁל, לְמָה הַדָּבָר דּוֹמֶה
steps.terutzResolutionType: Parable that redefines when jealousy happens
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Jealousy happens only toward an equal, so God being jealous of idols makes no sense.
steps.terutzMaskana: Jealousy is strongest toward a lesser replacement, so God's jealousy of worthless idols makes sense.

steps.title: זונין asks why people seem to be healed at idol temples
steps.stepSummary: זונין tells רבי עקיבא that they both know idols are powerless, yet people go to idols injured and come back healed. Why?
steps.simpleTranslation: זונין said to רבי עקיבא: My heart and your heart both know that idol worship has no substance. But we see people who go to it with broken limbs and come back whole! What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. זונין raises a puzzle about what people actually see happen. רבי עקיבא answers it in the next two steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both men agree that עבודה זרה has no real power. The problem is the evidence people see: sick people seem to get better after visiting idols. זונין wants to know how to explain this without giving the idol credit.

keyTerms.meaning: There is nothing real in it, no substance

phrases.english: Zunin said to Rabbi Akiva:
My heart and your heart know
that idol worship has no substance in it.
But we see people
who go there broken,
phrases.notes: He means people with injured limbs who go to the idol hoping to be healed.

phrases.english: and come back whole!
What is the reason?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ זוּנִין לְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: לִבִּי וְלִבָּךְ יָדַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story, still on the theme of idols having no real power.
steps.kashyaTarget: The shared belief that עבודה זרה has no power
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: People seem to be healed after going to idols, which looks like evidence that idols do have power.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא's parable of the trustworthy man
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא answers זונין with a parable: a trustworthy man refuses to deny a deposit, even though the depositor foolishly gave it without witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Let me tell you a parable. There was a trustworthy man in a city, and everyone left deposits with him without witnesses. One man always made his deposits in front of witnesses. One time that man forgot and made a deposit without witnesses. The trustworthy man's wife said: Come, let's deny he ever gave it. He answered her: Just because this fool acted wrongly, should we throw away our honesty?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא begins his answer to זונין's question with a story about honesty. The story sets up the explanation that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man who demanded witnesses did not trust the honest man, and once he made a deposit without them. The honest man still returns the deposit, because his honesty does not depend on how the other person behaves. This prepares the main idea: something good can happen to a person who acted wrongly, without his wrong act causing it.

keyTerms.meaning: Leaving deposits (money or items) for safekeeping
Let us deny it (claim it was never given)

phrases.english: He said to him: I will tell you a parable.
phrases.notes: רבי עקיבא is now answering זונין's question from the last step.

phrases.english: What is this matter like?
It is like a trustworthy man who lived in a city,

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל בְּנֵי עִירוֹ הָיוּ מַפְקִידִין אֶצְלוֹ
phrases.english: and all the people of his city would leave deposits with him
without witnesses,

phrases.aramaic: וּבָא אָדָם אֶחָד וְהִפְקִיד לוֹ בְּעֵדִים.
phrases.english: and one man came and made his deposits in front of witnesses.
One time he forgot
and made a deposit with him without witnesses.
His wife said to him: Come, let us deny it.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהּ: וְכִי מִפְּנֵי שֶׁשּׁוֹטֶה זֶה
phrases.english: He said to her: Just because this fool
acted improperly,
should we lose our trustworthiness?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: אֶמְשׁוֹל לְךָ מָשָׁל, לְמָה הַדָּבָר דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to זונין's question in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Parable that separates the healing from the person's wrong act
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Healing after visiting an idol suggests the idol has power.
steps.terutzMaskana: Just as the honest man stays honest regardless of the fool, the result is not caused by the fool's action.

steps.title: Sufferings keep their oath to leave on time
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא applies the parable: sufferings are sworn to leave at a set time, and they keep that oath even when the sick person has gone to an idol.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too with sufferings: when they are sent upon a person, they are made to swear: You will come only on this day, and leave only on this day, at this hour, through this person, and through this medicine. When their time to leave arrives, the sick man goes to an idol temple. The sufferings say: By right we should not leave. But then they say: Just because this fool is acting wrongly, should we break our oath?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא connects the parable to זונין's question and finishes his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The healing was already scheduled before the person ever went to the idol. The sufferings leave on time because they must keep their oath, just as the honest man kept his honesty. So the idol did nothing; it only looks as if it did because the timing happened to match.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי עקיבא, healing after visiting an idol is no proof of the idol's power. The illness was set to leave at that exact time anyway, and it keeps its oath even when the person acts wrongly.

phrases.english: So too with sufferings:
at the time they are sent upon a person,
they are made to swear:
that you will go to him only on such-and-such a day,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא תֵּצְאוּ אֶלָּא בְּיוֹם פְּלוֹנִי וּבְשָׁעָה פְּלוֹנִית,
phrases.english: and you will leave only on such-and-such a day and at such-and-such an hour,

phrases.aramaic: וְעַל יְדֵי פְּלוֹנִי וְעַל יְדֵי סַם פְּלוֹנִי.
phrases.english: through so-and-so and through such-and-such a medicine.
When their time to leave arrived,
this sick man went to an idol temple.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ יִסּוּרִין: דִּין הוּא שֶׁלֹּא נֵצֵא,
phrases.english: The sufferings said: By right we should not leave.
But then they say again:

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי מִפְּנֵי שֶׁשּׁוֹטֶה זֶה עוֹשֶׂה שֶׁלֹּא כַּהוֹגֶן
phrases.english: Just because this fool is acting improperly,
should we break our oath?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the parable from step 6 to the question in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the timing: the healing was already set and is not caused by the idol
steps.terutzMaskana: The sufferings left on their scheduled time because of their oath; the idol had no part in it.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן reads the פסוק about 'faithful' illnesses
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן's reading of a פסוק supports רבי עקיבא: illnesses are 'evil' in their mission but 'faithful' to their oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this matches what רבי יוחנן said: What is the meaning of the פסוק 'and evil and faithful sicknesses'? Evil in their mission, and faithful to their oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a teaching of רבי יוחנן that backs up רבי עקיבא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק calls illnesses both 'evil' and 'faithful,' which sounds strange. רבי יוחנן explains that they are 'evil' because their job is to cause harm, and 'faithful' because they keep their oath. That matches רבי עקיבא's idea that sufferings leave exactly when they swore to.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is (the same idea as)
What is the meaning of what is written
A mission, a job one is sent to do

phrases.english: And this is what Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
What is meant by what is written: "and evil and faithful sicknesses"?
"Evil" in their mission,
and "faithful" to their oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 7's idea that sufferings keep their oath.
steps.raayaObject: רבי עקיבא's claim that sufferings are bound by an oath about when they leave
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's reading of 'וחלים רעים ונאמנים' in דברים 28:59

steps.title: An idol that seems to bring rain after a human sacrifice
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר רב יצחק tells רב יהודה about an idol in his town that asks in a dream for a human sacrifice, and after it is done, rain really comes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא בר רב יצחק said to רב יהודה: There is an idol temple in our area. When the world needs rain, the idol appears to people in a dream and says: Slaughter a man for me and I will bring rain. They slaughter a man for it, and rain comes!
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge is raised: a case where an idol seems to really make something happen. This sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא's answer worked for illness, which was already set to end at a certain time. Here the idol actually makes a promise ahead of time, demands a sacrifice, and then rain follows. That looks much more like real power, so the question gets harder.

keyTerms.meaning: In our place, in our area

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא בַּר רַב יִצְחָק לְרַב יְהוּדָה:
phrases.english: Rava bar Rav Yitzḥak said to Rav Yehuda:
Isn't there an idol temple in our area,
where, when the world needs rain,
it appears to them in a dream and says to them:
Slaughter a man for me and I will bring rain.
They slaughter a man for it, and rain comes!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא בַּר רַב יִצְחָק לְרַב יְהוּדָה: הָאִיכָּא בֵּית עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה בְּאַתְרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a new case that רבי עקיבא's oath explanation does not obviously cover.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that idols have no real power and only seem to work by coincidence
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The idol announces ahead of time what it will do, demands a sacrifice, and then rain comes. That looks like real power, not just timing.

steps.title: Idol 'success' is allowed in order to mislead
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה explains, using רב's reading of a פסוק, that God lets idolaters be misled by apparent 'results' so that they will be driven out of the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Now, if I had died, I would not have been able to tell you this. As רב said: What does the פסוק mean, 'which the Lord your God allotted (חָלַק) to all the nations'? It teaches that He let them slip (הֶחְלִיקָן) through things, in order to drive them out of the world.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers רבא בר רב יצחק's question from step 9: why does rain really come after the idol's terrible sacrifice?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב reads the word חָלַק ('allotted') as if it said 'made slippery'. God lets idol worshippers see things that look like proof that the idol works. Those who choose idolatry are allowed to slide further into their mistake, so the rain is no proof that the idol has any power.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have died / been lying dead
He made them slip, misled them

steps.whyThisMatters: It gives a second, broader explanation for idols' apparent successes, beyond רבי עקיבא's answer about illness: even a striking 'result' that seems to be promised ahead of time does not show that an idol has any real power.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Now, if I had died,
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets. The word in square brackets is the corrected wording.

phrases.english: I would not have told you this matter,
as Rav said:
What is that which is written:
"which the Lord your God allotted
to all the nations"?
It teaches that He let them slip through things,
phrases.notes: It's a wordplay: חָלַק ('allotted') is read like 'made smooth' or slippery, so He was misleading them.

phrases.english: in order to drive them out of the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge about the idol that brings rain.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the event: the 'success' is a test meant to mislead, not real power.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Rain after the sacrifice might seem to show that the idol has power.
steps.terutzMaskana: God allows misleading signs so that those who choose idolatry are led astray.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: the path you choose is opened for you
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש's reading of a פסוק in משלי supports רב's idea: whoever comes to sin is given an opening, and whoever comes to purify himself is helped.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this matches what ריש לקיש said: What does the פסוק mean, 'If it concerns the scornful, He scorns them, and to the humble He gives grace'? One who comes to become impure is given an opening; one who comes to become pure is helped.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings ריש לקיש's teaching to show that רב's idea fits a wider principle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Heaven does not stop a person who chooses sin; it leaves the way open, as with the idolaters who are misled. But a person who chooses good gets active help. This backs up the idea that the idol's 'success' is just an open door for those who want it.

keyTerms.meaning: they open for him (they don't block him)

steps.whatToRemember: An idol's apparent 'results' prove nothing. God leaves an opening for those who choose sin and helps those who choose purity.

phrases.english: And this is what Reish Lakish said:
What is that which is written:
"If it concerns the scornful, He scorns them,
and to the humble He gives grace"?
One who comes to become impure — they open the way for him;
phrases.notes: 'Impure' here means choosing to sin, and 'they' means Heaven.

phrases.english: one who comes to become pure — they help him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב's teaching with a similar idea from ריש לקיש.
steps.raayaObject: רב's idea that idolaters are allowed to be misled

steps.title: Juice is not יין נסך until it reaches the vat
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: you may buy a trodden winepress from a נכרי even though he handled the grapes. The juice only becomes forbidden יין נסך once it flows down into the vat.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: We may buy a trodden winepress from a נכרי, even though he takes grapes in his hand and puts them on the pile. It does not become יין נסך until it goes down into the vat. Once it went down into the vat, what is in the vat is forbidden, and the rest is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a practical rule about wine-making with a נכרי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before the juice reaches the collecting vat, it does not count as wine yet, so the נכרי's touch does not make it יין נסך. Once juice reaches the vat, his touch forbids what is in the vat. Juice still in the press stays permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: a winepress whose grapes have been trodden
here: the heap of grapes in the press
wine forbidden because a נכרי's touch may have offered it to an idol
the collecting vat below the press

steps.confusionAlert: תַּפּוּחַ here does not mean 'apple'. It means the pile of grapes waiting to be trodden.

phrases.english: Mishnah:
We may buy a trodden winepress from a gentile,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא נוֹטֵל בְּיָדוֹ
phrases.english: even though he takes grapes in his hand
and puts them on the pile,
and it does not become libation wine
until it goes down into the vat.
Once it went down into the vat —
what is in the vat is forbidden,
and the rest is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ לוֹקְחִין גַּת בְּעוּטָה מִן הַנׇּכְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה; there is no link to the story before it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Grape juice becomes יין נסך only once it reaches the vat. What is in the vat is forbidden, and the rest stays permitted.

steps.title: Treading grapes together with a נכרי
steps.stepSummary: The משנה begins a new rule: a Jew may tread grapes in the winepress together with a נכרי.
steps.simpleTranslation: We may tread grapes with a נכרי in the winepress,
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens a second rule, which continues in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on the rule just taught: juice still in the press is not yet wine. So working alongside a נכרי there is allowed. The details of this rule come next.

phrases.english: We may tread with the gentile in the winepress,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The next clause of the same משנה, building on the vat rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Treading grapes together with a נכרי in the press is permitted.
